title: The Lutheran Epitome: Luther's 'purely passive' concerns the kindling of new motions
source_text: XL. Et eodem quoque redit doctrina Theologorum confessionis Augustanae. Quod Lutherus, inquiunt, scripsit hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere, id recte & dextre est accipiendum, videlicet, respectu divinae gratiae in accendendis novis motibus: hoc est, de eo intelligi oportet, quando spiritus Dei per verbum auditum, aut per usum Sacramentorum hominis voluntatem aggreditur, & conversionem atque regenerationem in homine operatur. Postquam enim Spiritus Sanctus hoc ipsum jam operatus est, atque effecit, hominisque voluntatem sola sua divina virtute & operatione immutavit atque renovavit: tunc revera hominis nova illa voluntas instrumentum est & organum Dei Spiritus Sancti, ut ea non modo gratiam apprehendat, verum etiam in operibus sequentibus Spiritui Sancto cooperetur. In Epitome articulorum de quibus controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos Confessionis Augustanae art. 2. qui est de libero arbitrio.
pass_a_gloss: XL. And to the same also comes the doctrine of the Theologians of the Augsburg confession. That Luther, they say, wrote that the will of man in conversion behaves purely passively, is to be taken rightly and properly, namely, in respect of divine grace in kindling new motions: that is, it must be understood of when the spirit of God, through the word heard, or through the use of the Sacraments, approaches the will of man, and works conversion and regeneration in man. For after the Holy Spirit has already wrought and effected this very thing, and has changed and renewed the will of man by his divine power and operation alone: then truly that new will of man is the instrument and organ of God the Holy Spirit, so that by it not only does he apprehend grace, but also in the following works cooperates with the Holy Spirit. In the Epitome of the articles about which controversies arose among the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession art. 2. which is on free choice.
pass_b_english: The teaching of the theologians of the Augsburg Confession comes to the same thing. 'Luther's statement,' they say, 'that man's will is purely passive in conversion must be taken in the right and proper sense: with respect to divine grace kindling new motions. It refers to the moment when God's Spirit, through the word heard or the use of the sacraments, takes hold of man's will and works conversion and regeneration in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has done and accomplished this, and has changed and renewed man's will by his divine power and working alone, then man's new will really is an instrument and organ of God the Holy Spirit: so that it not only lays hold of grace but also cooperates with the Holy Spirit in the works that follow.' Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, article 2, on free choice.
